before.definition: Memory the operating system uses to keep recently read file data. A PostgreSQL read from outside shared buffers may be served from here without touching the disk.
before.example: A 'read' in EXPLAIN BUFFERS can take microseconds if the page is in the OS cache.

after.definition: Memory the operating system uses to keep recently read file data. A PostgreSQL read from outside shared buffers may be served from here without touching the disk.
after.example: An EXPLAIN BUFFERS read counts access outside PostgreSQL shared buffers; the OS may already have the requested file page in memory.

corrections.reason: Consolidate the later local canonical label with the exact independently reviewed Query owner; qualify actual own prose as table heap or OS page cache, preserving the precise storage concept and avoiding algorithmic heaps/generic caches.

before.definition: A row version that has been replaced or deleted and that no running snapshot can still see. It wastes space until VACUUM marks its space reusable.
before.example: pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup shows roughly how many dead tuples each table holds.

after.definition: An obsolete row version that is no longer visible to any snapshot the server must preserve. Its storage can be reclaimed by vacuum or, where applicable, page pruning; an old version still needed by a snapshot is not yet removable.
after.example: pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup is an estimate of dead row versions; it is not an exact count of distinct deleted logical rows.

before.definition: A workload dominated by adding rows rather than changing older rows. Increasing values such as timestamps may correlate with storage location, which can make BRIN useful; append-heavy alone does not guarantee physical ordering.
before.example: An append-heavy sensor log may suit BRIN when its time values stay correlated with heap position.

after.definition: A workload dominated by adding rows rather than changing older rows. Increasing values such as timestamps may correlate with storage location, which can make BRIN useful; append-heavy alone does not guarantee physical ordering. An append-only workload specifically forbids changes to existing records.
after.example: An append-heavy sensor log may suit BRIN when its time values stay correlated with heap position.

before.definition: Query plan steps such as sorts, hash joins and hash aggregation that need working memory. A sort has a work_mem base allowance; hash operations use work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier, and multiple operations or parallel workers can multiply consumption.
before.example: A query that hash-joins two tables and then sorts the result runs two such operations at once.

after.definition: Query plan steps such as sorts, hash joins and hash aggregation that need working memory. A sort has a work_mem base allowance; hash operations use work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier, and multiple operations or parallel workers can multiply consumption.
after.example: A hash join followed by a sort uses working-memory plan operations; which allocations overlap and their sizes depend on the execution plan.

before.definition: The XID age at which PostgreSQL forces an anti-wraparound vacuum of a table, even if autovacuum is disabled. Default 200 million transactions.
before.example: 200 million is under a tenth of the roughly 2.1 billion XID comparison horizon.

after.definition: The allocated-XID age that a table's oldest-unfrozen-XID boundary can reach before PostgreSQL forces an anti-wraparound vacuum, even if ordinary autovacuum is disabled. The PostgreSQL 18 default is 200 million allocated transaction IDs; this is not elapsed time or a count of committed top-level transactions.
after.example: 200 million is under a tenth of the roughly 2.1 billion XID comparison horizon.

before.definition: The failure that would occur when the 32-bit XID counter cycles around: old rows would appear to be in the future and vanish. VACUUM prevents it by freezing old row versions before they are about 2 billion transactions old.
before.example: A server doing 1,000 writing transactions a second uses 2 billion XIDs in about 23 days.

after.definition: The visibility failure that old unfrozen committed insertions could suffer when normal 32-bit XIDs advance beyond their approximately half-range safe ordering window. Freezing protects those old insertions before they become too old for normal comparisons.
after.example: At exactly 1,000 allocated normal XIDs per second, two billion IDs take about 23 days; subtransactions can increase ID consumption beyond a top-level transaction rate.

before.definition: The maximum number of concurrent connections allowed. In PostgreSQL the server's limit on client connections is set by max_connections (default 100); each connection costs a backend process and memory, so raising it is not free.
before.example: With max_connections = 100, a 101st simultaneous connection is refused; ordinary roles are refused a few slots earlier, because superuser_reserved_connections (default 3) keeps some for superusers.

after.definition: A configured maximum number of simultaneous connections to a service. PostgreSQL's max_connections controls its client-connection cap (typically 100 by default); each connection normally needs a backend process and memory, and reserved slots reduce the capacity available to ordinary roles.
after.example: With max_connections set to 100, no more than 100 client connections fit. The default three superuser-reserved slots and any additional reserved_connections slots reduce the number available to an ordinary role.

before.definition: A permission granted to a role on an object, such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table. Without the privilege the operation fails.
before.example: GRANT SELECT ON events TO reporting gives the reporting role read access only.

after.definition: A permission granted to a role on an object, such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table. Without the privilege the operation fails.
after.example: GRANT SELECT ON events TO reporting grants table-read access; the role still needs applicable database and schema access, and its other grants determine what else it can do.

before.definition: PostgreSQL's own cache of table and index pages in shared memory, used by every backend. Its size is set by shared_buffers, typically 128 MB by default; a page not found there is requested from the operating system.
before.example: Production servers often set shared_buffers to around a quarter of RAM.

after.definition: PostgreSQL's own cache of table and index pages in shared memory, used by every backend. Its size is set by shared_buffers, typically 128 MB by default; a page not found there is requested from the operating system.
after.example: For a dedicated database server with at least 1 GB of RAM, the PostgreSQL manual suggests 25% of RAM as a starting value, followed by workload-specific measurement.

before.definition: A copy of the whole cluster's data files taken while it runs, usually with pg_basebackup. Combined with archived WAL it is the starting point for point-in-time recovery.
before.example: pg_basebackup -D /backups/base copies the data directory from a running server.

after.definition: A physical copy of a PostgreSQL cluster's data files. pg_basebackup can produce one while the server runs; together with the WAL needed to make it consistent and reach a target, a suitable base backup is the starting point for point-in-time recovery.
after.example: pg_basebackup -D /backups/base copies the data directory from a running server.

before.definition: A PostgreSQL role that bypasses almost all permission checks, except the right to log in. Applications should use a non-superuser role with only the privileges they need.
before.example: The bootstrap role created by initdb is a superuser; its name need not be postgres.

after.definition: A PostgreSQL role that bypasses almost all permission checks, except the right to log in. Applications should use a non-superuser role with only the privileges they need.
after.example: The bootstrap role created by initdb is a superuser; its name need not be postgres.

corrections.reason: A non-superuser is not an alias for the opposite privilege status.

after.definition: A named namespace inside one PostgreSQL database, containing objects such as tables, types and functions. Different schemas can contain objects with the same name; privileges govern access. This is distinct from the general use of schema to mean the design of a database.
after.example: public.orders and billing.orders identify two separate tables in two schemas of the same database.

corrections.reason: Precise namespace/negative-role meaning avoids wrong donor sense.

after.definition: A PostgreSQL role without the SUPERUSER attribute. It is subject to normal privilege checks, but its granted privileges and other role attributes still determine its powers; lacking SUPERUSER alone does not make it least-privileged.
after.example: An application role should lack SUPERUSER and receive only the database, schema, table and sequence privileges its operations require.

corrections.reason: Precise namespace/negative-role meaning avoids wrong donor sense.

before.definition: The setting controlling what COMMIT waits for before returning: local WAL flush (the default, on), nothing (off) or, with synchronous standbys, their acknowledgement.
before.example: SET synchronous_commit = off speeds commits but risks losing the most recent ones in a crash.

after.definition: A commit acknowledgement that waits for the configured persistence or replica conditions before returning. PostgreSQL's synchronous_commit setting selects local WAL and optional standby waits: on normally waits for local WAL flush and any configured synchronous-standby feedback, while off can return before local WAL flush.
after.example: SET synchronous_commit = off speeds commits but risks losing the most recent ones in a crash.

corrections.reason: off skips commit WAL-flush wait; it does not remove all work or all waits.

before.definition: Searching natural-language documents for words, ignoring word endings and ranking matches, rather than exact string comparison. PostgreSQL implements it with tsvector and tsquery types, often indexed with GIN.
before.example: A search for 'workshops' can match a document containing 'workshop'.

after.definition: Searching natural-language documents using parsed and normalised search terms rather than only exact string comparison. PostgreSQL provides configurable dictionaries, word-form normalisation and ranking functions, with tsvector and tsquery types and optional GIN indexes.
after.example: With PostgreSQL's English text-search configuration, a search for 'workshops' can match a document containing 'workshop'.

corrections.reason: Stemming and ranking are configured capabilities, not universal mandatory behaviour.

before.definition: A run of consecutive table pages (PostgreSQL's 8 kB storage blocks) that a BRIN index summarises as one unit; 128 pages by default.
before.example: With the default 128 pages per range, one BRIN entry covers about 1 MB of table.

after.definition: A run of consecutive PostgreSQL table pages that a BRIN index summarises as one unit. The default pages_per_range is 128; a standard-build page is 8 kB, but the build-time block size can differ.
after.example: With the default 128 pages per range, one BRIN entry covers about 1 MB of table.

corrections.reason: 8kB is the default, not the only possible PostgreSQL block size.

before.definition: A system view listing the locks held and awaited by every session. Joining it with pg_stat_activity (or using pg_blocking_pids) shows who blocks whom.
before.example: SELECT pg_blocking_pids(1234); lists the sessions blocking process 1234.

after.definition: A system view of outstanding server lock requests, including held and awaited locks. Row-lock ownership is normally recorded on disk rather than listed directly here; a session waiting on a row often appears as waiting for the holder’s transaction ID. Use pg_blocking_pids with pg_stat_activity to investigate blockers.
after.example: SELECT pg_blocking_pids(1234); lists the sessions blocking process 1234.

corrections.reason: pg_locks does not normally expose every held row-level lock as a tuple record.

before.definition: A copy of a database kept up to date from another server; in PostgreSQL usually a standby fed by streaming replication.
before.example: A read replica in another data centre serves queries and is ready for failover.

after.definition: A copy of a database kept up to date from another server; in PostgreSQL usually a standby fed by streaming replication.
after.example: A read replica in another data centre can serve queries; promotion and acceptable failover data loss require an explicit operational plan.

corrections.reason: A read replica is not automatically proved ready for correct failover.

before.definition: Replication where the primary acknowledges a commit without waiting for any standby. It is fast, but standbys lag and a failover can lose recently acknowledged commits.
before.example: A standby 2 seconds behind can lose 2 seconds of commits if it is promoted after the primary dies.

after.definition: Replication where the primary can acknowledge a commit without waiting for a standby acknowledgement. Standbys can lag, and failover can lose acknowledged commits that the promoted standby has not received.
after.example: A standby 2 seconds behind can lose 2 seconds of commits if it is promoted after the primary dies.

corrections.reason: Correct unconditional speed and chronology claims to acknowledgement-independent PostgreSQL semantics. Use a qualified canonical label to retain the precise local entry rather than merging it with an earlier broad same-name owner; valid local aliases cover the unchanged body and q11 prompt.

before.definition: Restoring a base backup, then replaying archived WAL up to a chosen target such as a timestamp, to recover the database as it was at that moment.
before.example: Recover to 14:02:59 to get back the rows deleted at 14:03.

after.definition: Restoring a suitable physical base backup and replaying the required continuous WAL to a configured target, such as a timestamp. The target must be after the base backup finished; inclusive/exclusive target settings determine which boundary transaction is included.
after.example: Recover to 14:02:59 to get back the rows deleted at 14:03.

corrections.reason: Recovery cannot stop within the base-backup interval; include end-of-backup prerequisite in body and original q12 workedExample.

before.definition: A database run for you by a cloud provider, such as Amazon RDS, which automates backups, patches and failover. You still need to know its retention and recovery guarantees.
before.example: As documented in October 2026, Amazon RDS DB instances allow automated-backup retention from 0 to 35 days; DB clusters have different limits and support depends on the deployment.

after.definition: A database service operated by a provider that automates selected tasks such as backups and patching. Failover features and guarantees depend on the chosen deployment; the user still needs to understand retention, recovery and availability limits.
after.example: As documented in October 2026, Amazon RDS DB instances allow automated-backup retention from 0 to 35 days; DB clusters have different limits and support depends on the deployment.

corrections.reason: Automated failover is deployment-dependent, not a guarantee of every managed database.

---
id: pg-autovacuum-thresholds
title: Understand autovacuum thresholds
level: intermediate
minutes: 4
sourceLesson: postgresql-in-practice
summary: The dead-tuple threshold scales with estimated table size.
---

This unit uses PostgreSQL 18 defaults. PostgreSQL 16 and 17 have no `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` cap. These are eligibility thresholds, not promises that a worker starts immediately.

## Size-dependent cleanup

Autovacuum does not clean a table after every update. It waits until enough dead row versions have built up to make the work worthwhile, and the point at which it acts grows with the table. In PostgreSQL 18 the rule is below; the cap, `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold`, is new in version 18.

```formula
T_vac = min(T_max, T_base + sN)
T_vac = min(10^8, 50 + 0.2 × 10^6)
T_vac = min(10^8, 200050)
T_vac = 200050 tuples
where
T_vac: the vacuum threshold: autovacuum vacuums the table when the estimated dead-tuple count exceeds this; worker availability and other triggers also matter
min: the minimum function: whichever of its two inputs is smaller
T_max: autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold, a cap that stops the threshold growing without limit on huge tables; default 100,000,000 (10^8) tuples
T_base: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, a fixed number of changed rows always required, so tiny tables are not vacuumed after every change; default 50 tuples
s: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor, the fraction of the table that may be dead before vacuum starts; default 0.2 (20 %), no unit
N: the estimated number of rows in the table, kept in pg_class.reltuples and refreshed by VACUUM and ANALYZE; here 1,000,000 (10^6)
tuples: the unit counted here: row versions, which PostgreSQL calls tuples
In words: with these PostgreSQL 18 defaults, the dead-tuple eligibility threshold is fifty plus a fifth of the estimated row count, capped at one hundred million.
```

So a 1,000,000-row table passes this dead-tuple threshold when its estimated dead-version count exceeds 200,050. Repeated updates to the same logical row can leave several obsolete versions. This is not a count of distinct rows, and an eligible table may wait for a worker. For anything above a few hundred rows the 20 % term dominates; the fixed 50 only matters for tiny tables. The cap only matters for very large tables: a 1,000,000,000-row table would otherwise wait for 200 million dead rows, but with the cap the threshold is capped at 100 million dead versions.

The threshold is checked, not a start-time guarantee: `autovacuum_naptime` defaults to one minute between autovacuum runs on a database. Worker availability and a running worker's progress also matter. Similar rules start a vacuum after many inserts (`autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold`, 1,000 rows by default, plus 20 % of the table's not-yet-frozen part) and start ANALYZE (50 rows plus 10 % of the estimated table size by default, counting inserts, updates and deletes). A large, busy table often needs a smaller vacuum scale factor of its own, set per table as a storage parameter, for example `ALTER TABLE bookings SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01)`.

## Key takeaways

- The dead-tuple threshold scales with estimated table size.
- PostgreSQL 18 adds a configurable maximum threshold.
- Worker availability and checks determine when eligible work runs.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/routine-vacuuming.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: runtime config vacuum](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-vacuum.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: sql createtable](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html)

corrections: V1 pg-vacuum-snapshots-statistics: 'a replication slot whose consumer has stopped reading' was listed as holding back table cleanup. Executed: a stale logical slot (catalog_xmin only) and a physical slot without feedback xmin both let VACUUM remove all 10,000 dead versions. Now: a slot that still records an old xmin from a standby that stopped connecting; logical slots hold back only system-catalog cleanup and WAL; check xmin or catalog_xmin; takeaway says slots with an old xmin.

V2 glossary autovacuum-vacuum-scale-factor: author's new bare alias 'scale factor' falls back across subjects (databases precedes synth), so system-design/11's unit-conversion 'scale factor' would have opened the autovacuum entry instead of synth's scale-factor. Alias removed (entry back to baseline); the 4 lesson uses and 3 question uses now say 'vacuum scale factor', an existing alias.
V3 glossary pg-stat-user-tables (new): fully shadowed by databases/04 pg-stat-user-indexes, which owns 'pg_stat_user_tables'; a dead new duplicate fails the release dictionary check. Removed.

V4 glossary pg-hot-standby-feedback: 'It prevents those queries being cancelled' overstated; the docs say it eliminates cancels caused by cleanup records. Now: stops cancellations caused by the primary cleaning up rows they were reading.

V5 glossary pg-postmaster: 'restarts the other processes if one crashes' was imprecise. Executed SIGKILL of one backend: every other session was terminated and the server reinitialised. Now says exactly that.

V6 pg-autovacuum-thresholds-q1 distractor 3 explanation claimed disabling autovacuum lets 'wraparound risk build all day'; anti-wraparound vacuums still run when autovacuum is off. Now: dead versions build up and automatic ANALYZE stops.

H2 pg-clients-backends-pools: undated 'run on PostgreSQL 18' now says 18.6, and that in October 2026 18 was current and PostgreSQL 19 had reached its first release candidate (2026-10-15).

lowConfidence.claim: With many distinct leading values, a separate index on the later column is still the better fit than relying on skip scan.
lowConfidence.reason: indexes-multicolumn says skip scan is generally chosen only with few distinct leading values and the planner otherwise prefers a sequential scan (confirmed by execution); recommending a separate index is sound design inference rather than a quoted rule.

lowConfidence.claim: Experiment figures (about a dozen pages, 2,942 pages, ~7,700 rows, 53 index searches, 360/1,416 kB, 9,976 kB spill, 24,788 kB quicksort, ~8 MB hash).
lowConfidence.reason: Reproduced on 18.6/aarch64 (most exactly); they depend on version, platform, data and timing and are presented as one test run.

lowConfidence.claim: Insert threshold: '20 % of the rows in the part of the table not yet frozen'.
lowConfidence.reason: PG 18 formula multiplies reltuples by the fraction of pages not all-frozen (1 - relallfrozen/relpages); the lesson's row-based phrasing is a faithful approximation, not the exact page-based definition.

lowConfidence.claim: PostgreSQL 18 is the current major release; PostgreSQL 19 is at release-candidate stage.
lowConfidence.reason: True on 2026-10-30 (postgresql.org) and dated in the text, but time-sensitive: 19 GA is likely soon.

pg-clients-backends-pools.rationale: Author added the process-per-connection mechanism, max_connections and pooling rationale. Re-checked: postmaster as 'supervisor process' spawning a backend per connection (connect-estab, tutorial-arch); max_connections boot value 100 executed ('typically 100' per docs). Verifier dated the version statement: examples on 18.6; in October 2026 18 is the current major release and PostgreSQL 19 reached RC1 on 2026-10-15 (postgresql.org front page/news). No formula before or after. Restaurant-waiter analogy kept (maps backend per connection, pool, transaction pooling losing session state; limit accurate). q1 unchanged and re-checked (server enforces constraints and row locking).

pg-ticket-schema-types.rationale: Schema SQL executed unchanged on 18.6, and the CREATE TABLE/INSERT part also on 16 and 17 images: CHECK accepts NULL without NOT NULL, identity gap after rollback (2 skipped), only PK and UNIQUE indexes created (event_id unindexed), timestamptz 11:00+01 London / 19:00+09 Tokyo, uuidv7() version 7 (PG 18 release notes). TV-listings analogy times recomputed (19:00 UTC = 20:00 BST = 04:00 JST next day). No formula. q2/q3 unchanged; q2 distractors executed (DEFAULT 0 and UNIQUE both accept NULL/negative).

pg-conditional-seat-reservation.rationale: Race executed in my container: Read Committed loser waits, rechecks and returns 0 rows (seats stay 0); Repeatable Read loser gets 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'. RETURNING old/new executed (2 -> 1) and matches PG 18 release note that earlier versions returned only new values for UPDATE. Box-office analogy kept (clear mapping of read-then-write vs conditional UPDATE; limit correct). No formula. q4 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-booking-rollback-idempotency.rationale: Executed the commit path, the buggy decrement + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING + COMMIT (seats 4 -> 3 with one booking), the aborted-transaction error and savepoint recovery. Body text was already correct. Verifier removed the author's bakery analogy: its limit ('the baker cannot un-crack eggs') contradicts its own 'put the eggs back = ROLLBACK' mapping, the box-office analogy in the previous unit already covers the shop setting, and the lesson is a short procedure the CLAUDE.md rule says not to force an analogy onto. No formula. q5 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-snapshots-write-skew-retries.rationale: Executed on-call write skew: both Repeatable Read transactions commit (both inactive); under Serializable the second fails with 'read/write dependencies ... pivot, during commit attempt' (SQLSTATE 40001 family). Snapshot-start rule checked against transaction-iso ('first non-transaction-control statement'). Rota-photo analogy kept (good mapping; limit that a snapshot is a visibility rule is accurate). No formula. q9 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-query-indexes-explain.rationale: Rebuilt 400,000 bookings over 52 events: composite index Index Scan + Limit with 11 shared hits (author 14) and no Sort; without it a Parallel Seq Scan over exactly 2,942 pages plus top-N heapsort of 7,692 rows (author 7,693); Index Scan Backward for ASC; tiny table Seq Scan + Sort; skip scan 'Index Searches: 53' for 52 distinct events; with a high-cardinality leading column the planner seq-scans. PG 18 EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed Buffers without the option (release-18, sql-explain). Verifier hedged the data-dependent figures to 'about a dozen pages' and 'roughly 7,700 rows'. Skip-scan guidance matches indexes-multicolumn ('so few distinct x values'). No formula. q6/q7 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-jsonb-relational-boundaries.rationale: Executed: containment query; '{"a": 2, "a": 3}'::jsonb -> {"a": 3}, json keeps input text; 200,000 docs: 200-row @> uses Bitmap Index Scan on GIN, near-all-rows @> uses Seq Scan; a B-tree on the jsonb column never gives an @> Index Cond (even with enable_seqscan off it only full-scans the index and filters). Printed-form analogy kept (limit notes JSONB is queryable and normalised). No formula. q8 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-vacuum-snapshots-statistics.rationale: Executed every horizon case: idle RR after SELECT holds backend_xmin and blocks (0 removed, 10000 dead but not removable), also when its SELECT read a different table; idle RC after only a SELECT holds nothing (10000 removed); idle RC after a write holds an XID and blocks; RR or a writer in another database does not block; a disconnected prepared transaction blocks until ROLLBACK PREPARED (second container, max_prepared_transactions=5); bloat 360 kB -> 1,416 kB -> stays 1,416 kB after 30,000 removed -> reused -> VACUUM FULL 360 kB. procarray.c (REL_18_STABLE) confirms other databases are ignored for non-shared horizons, so the analogy limit 'every table of that database' is correct. Verifier correction: a stale logical slot (catalog_xmin only) and a physical slot with no feedback xmin did NOT block user-table cleanup in tests, so the slot bullet, the pg_replication_slots check (now xmin or catalog_xmin) and the takeaway now name slots that record an old xmin. HOT/BRIN 'since PostgreSQL 16' matches release-16 and storage-hot. No formula. q10 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-autovacuum-thresholds.rationale: Kept T_vac = min(T_max, T_base + sN) as the one essential formula: the size-proportional threshold is the lesson's objective, and its definitions match routine-vacuuming 25.1.6 exactly; all defaults executed (50, 0.2, 1e8, 1000/0.2 insert, 50/0.1 analyse, naptime 60 s, 3 workers, 2 ms delay). Prose ladder recomputed (250; 200,050; 10,000,050; cap binds above ~500M rows). Insert threshold confirmed against the PG 18 formula (reltuples x (1 - relallfrozen/relpages)); verifier added 'inserted since the last vacuum'. Verifier removed the author's bare 'scale factor' alias (see corrections) and reworded the four prose uses and the question to 'vacuum scale factor'. Office-cleaner analogy kept (adds worker limit and naptime mapping; limit accurate). q1 rewrite accepted; verifier fixed one distractor explanation.

questionsRewritten.pg-autovacuum-thresholds-q1: Author rewrote a threshold substitution (1M rows -> 200,050, with a formula card) into a configuration decision for a 50M-row table: per-table scale factor 0.01 (~500,050) vs raising the base, raising naptime, or disabling autovacuum with nightly VACUUM FULL. Verifier checked the key and every distractor; changed 'scale factor' to 'vacuum scale factor' (alias removal) and corrected distractor 3's explanation, which claimed wraparound risk builds all day although anti-wraparound vacuums still run with autovacuum off; it now says automatic ANALYZE also stops.

pg-xid-freezing-wraparound.rationale: Removed 2^32/2 formula judged redundant (prose states ~4.3 billion values, ~2.1 billion each way; recomputed 4,294,967,296 and 2,147,483,648). Executed: no XID after a SELECT, XID after UPDATE, pg_current_xact_id() assigns one, VACUUM FREEZE sets age 0, frozen row still updatable. 40-million warning, 3-million refusal with read-only transactions allowed, 200M autovacuum_freeze_max_age and the advice against stopping the postmaster/single-user mode all match routine-vacuuming 24.1.5. Verifier reworded two 'read-only' phrases that linked to a React dictionary entry. 12-hour-clock analogy kept; its example times recomputed. q1 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-wal-replicas-durability.rationale: Checked against wal-intro (sequential WAL much cheaper to sync than data pages), wal-async-commit (loss window up to 3 x wal_writer_delay, consistent as if aborted), runtime-config-wal (fsync=off unrecoverable corruption; synchronous_commit on = standby flushed, remote_apply = applied/visible) and warm-standby. Defaults executed (synchronous_commit on, fsync on, wal_writer_delay 200 ms). Till-roll analogy kept (limit about low-level page records and flush is accurate). No formula. q11 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-backups-point-in-time-recovery.rationale: Checked: continuous archiving restores only an entire cluster, and the stop point must be after the base backup's end (continuous-archiving); pg_dump dumps one database, roles/tablespaces need pg_dumpall (app-pgdump). Document version-history analogy kept (limit: whole-cluster forward replay). No formula. q12 unchanged and re-checked.

pg-troubleshooting-query-memory.rationale: Executed: blocked second booking shows wait_event_type Lock / transactionid with pg_blocking_pids = first pid; sort of 400,000 strings external merge Disk 9976kB at 4 MB vs quicksort Memory 24788kB with SET LOCAL 64MB (exact match); HashAggregate 8281 kB at multiplier 2.0 and 4249 kB at 1.0; SIGKILL of one backend made the bystander session get 'terminating connection because of crash of another server process' and the postmaster reinitialised (restart_after_crash on). Per-worker work_mem confirmed verbatim in runtime-config-resource. Reference formula M_sort = wkc kept as optional budgeting card (In words stands alone); 4x3x100 = 1,200 MB ~1.2 GB and 64x3x100 = 19,200 MB ~19 GB recomputed. Kitchen-bench analogy kept. q1 rewrite accepted.

questionsRewritten.pg-troubleshooting-query-memory-q1: Author replaced a 4 MB x 3 x 100 multiplication (with a formula card) by a configuration-risk diagnosis: raising work_mem to 256 MB globally for one report on a 150-session server; the key (multiplying memory, use SET LOCAL or a role setting) and the three misconception distractors (shared pool, up-front reservation, hashes exempt) were checked against runtime-config-resource and executed spills. No verifier change.

pg-clients-backends-pools.rationale: Restaurant waiters: waiter = backend process per connection, kitchen = shared memory/storage, fixed team = pool, different waiter per course = transaction pooling losing session state. Limit (a backend serves one connection for life; extra backends compete for CPU/memory/locks) matches connect-estab and runtime-config-connection.

pg-ticket-schema-types.rationale: TV listings for a live broadcast: kick-off = stored instant, listing page = session time zone, weekly 9am London show = named zone plus recurrence. Times recomputed (19:00 UTC = 20:00 BST = 04:00 JST next day). Limit (timestamptz keeps no zone name or offset) matches datatype-datetime and execution.

pg-conditional-seat-reservation.rationale: Box office last ticket: deciding at home = read-then-write in app code, clerk checking the drawer = WHERE in the UPDATE, single window = row lock. Limit (RC rechecks the new committed row, RR errors) executed.

pg-booking-rollback-idempotency.rationale: Author's bakery order-slip analogy removed by the verifier: its limit ('cannot un-crack eggs') contradicted its own 'putting the eggs back = ROLLBACK' mapping, the previous unit's box-office analogy already covers the shop setting, and the lesson is a short commit/rollback procedure with a concrete bug that the main text explains directly.

pg-snapshots-write-skew-retries.rationale: Two photos of the on-call whiteboard: photo = RR snapshot, rubbing out different names = updating different rows, empty board = broken invariant. Limit (snapshot is a visibility rule; SSI tracks read/write dependencies) matches transaction-iso and executed Serializable failure.

pg-query-indexes-explain.rationale: Filing cabinet with a drawer per event, folders newest first: drawer = leading event_id, order = created_at DESC, front 20 = Index Scan feeding LIMIT. Limit (B-tree pages, planner may scan, backward scans) executed (Index Scan Backward for ASC). Backward-scan fact is not needed by any question.

pg-jsonb-relational-boundaries.rationale: Printed form with a notes section: boxes = constrained typed columns, notes = JSONB with no type or presence check. Limit (JSONB is queryable, GIN-indexable and normalised) executed.

pg-vacuum-snapshots-statistics.rationale: Library keeping old editions while early visitors remain: editions = row versions, earliest visitor = oldest snapshot/horizon, free-shelf list = plain VACUUM, new bookcase = VACUUM FULL. Limit 'one old snapshot holds back cleanup in every table of that database' executed (RR reading another table blocked vt; a session in another database did not) and confirmed in procarray.c; slots/standbys also count.

pg-autovacuum-thresholds.rationale: Office cleaner visiting once a fifth of desks are messy, three cleaners on a one-minute round: fraction = vacuum scale factor, room size = row count, cleaners = autovacuum_max_workers, round = naptime, per-room rule = per-table setting. Limit (estimated counts, fixed base of 50, snapshot-held versions) matches routine-vacuuming; worded to avoid the removed 'scale factor' alias.

pg-xid-freezing-wraparound.rationale: 12-hour clock: clock time = 32-bit XID, half the dial = ~2.1-billion past window, 'long ago' stamp = freezing. Example times recomputed. Limit (counter advances with XID assignment, not elapsed time) executed (SELECT-only transaction gets no XID).

pg-wal-replicas-durability.rationale: Shop till roll: roll = WAL, stock cards = data pages, last card update = checkpoint, branch receiving roll copies = streaming standby. Limit (WAL records low-level page changes and is safe only once flushed) matches wal-intro and wal-reliability.

pg-backups-point-in-time-recovery.rationale: Shared document mirror vs version history: mirror = standby copying mistakes, history = base backup plus archived WAL, chosen time = recovery target. Limit (whole cluster rebuilt by forward replay) matches continuous-archiving.

pg-troubleshooting-query-memory.rationale: Kitchen workbench per chopping job with corridor trolleys: bench = work_mem per sort, trolleys = temp-file spill, cooks = sessions, jobs = sorts. Limit (OOM kill can disrupt every session; allowance not reserved) executed (backend SIGKILL terminated a bystander session and reinitialised the server).
